prompt: Which of these statements are **true**? Select all that apply. (n is the input size; O is an upper bound on growth, Θ a tight bound; log2 and log10 are logarithms to base 2 and base 10.)

options.text: Linear has a quadratic upper bound
options.explanation:
True. A quadratic upper bound covers linear work.

```formula
n ≤ n^2 for n ≥ 1
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: A quadratic upper bound covers linear work.
```

options.text: Quadratic has a linear upper bound
options.explanation:
False. The ratio grows without limit, so no fixed linear multiplier suffices.

```formula
n^2 / n = n → ∞
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
→: "tends to" as n grows
∞: infinity: growing without limit
In words: The ratio grows without limit, so no fixed linear multiplier suffices.
```

options.text: Twice input plus five has tight linear growth
options.explanation:
True. Fixed linear multiples squeeze the function.

```formula
2n ≤ 2n + 5 ≤ 7n for n ≥ 1
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
<, >, ≤, ≥: less than, greater than, at most, at least
In words: Fixed linear multiples squeeze the function.
```

options.text: Base-two and base-ten logs have the same tight growth
options.explanation:
True. Changing a log base multiplies the value by a fixed factor.

```formula
log_2(n) / log_10(n) ≈ 3.32
where
log_10: the base-ten logarithm
log_2: the base-two logarithm
n: the input size, a positive whole number
≈: approximately equal to (here exactly 1 / log_10(2) for every n > 1)
In words: Changing a log base multiplies the value by a fixed factor.
```

options.text: Base-three exponential has a base-two exponential upper bound
options.explanation:
False. Changing the exponential base leaves an unbounded ratio.

```formula
3^n / 2^n = 1.5^n → ∞
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
→: "tends to" as n grows
∞: infinity: growing without limit
In words: Changing the exponential base leaves an unbounded ratio.
```

workedExample:
Test each claim with the ratio of the left side to the right side as n grows:

```formula
r(n) = f(n) / g(n)
n / n^2 = 1 / n → 0
n^2 / n = n → ∞
(2n + 5) / n → 2
log_2(n) / log_10(n) ≈ 3.32
3^n / 2^n = 1.5^n → ∞
where
r(n): the ratio of the left-hand function to the right-hand one
f(n): the left-hand function in the claim
g(n): the right-hand function inside O or Θ
n: the input size, a positive whole number
log_2(n), log_10(n): the logarithms of n to base 2 and base 10
→: "tends to" as n grows
∞: infinity: growing without limit
≈: approximately equal to (here exactly 1 / log_10(2) for every n > 1)
In words: f = O(g) needs this ratio to stay below some fixed number; f = Θ(g) also needs it to stay above some fixed positive number.
```

| First | tends to zero | true |
| Second | grows forever | false |
| Third | tends to two | true |
| Fourth | about 3.32 | true |
| Fifth | grows forever | false |

prompt: Which listed function does **not** have an O(2^n) upper bound? Here n is the input size, and O means an eventual upper bound up to a fixed factor.

options.text: Base two to one more than input
options.explanation:
This has the bound: increasing the exponent by one gives only a fixed factor of two.

```formula
2^{n+1} = 2 × 2^n
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
In words: This has the bound: increasing the exponent by one gives only a fixed factor of two.
```

options.text: Base two to input, plus input’s fifth power
options.explanation:
This has the bound: a fixed fifth power is eventually negligible beside the base-two exponential.

```formula
f(n) = 2^n + n^5
n^5 / 2^n → 0
where
f: the function being compared
n: the input size, a positive whole number
→: "tends to" as n grows
In words: This has the bound: a fixed fifth power is eventually negligible beside the base-two exponential.
```

This has the bound: a fixed tenth power loses to an exponential eventually, even if it is large for small inputs.

```formula
f(n) = n^{10}
n^{10} / 2^n → 0
where
f: the function being compared
n: the input size, a positive whole number
→: "tends to" as n grows
In words: This has the bound: a fixed tenth power loses to an exponential eventually, even if it is large for small inputs.
```

Correct: this does not have the bound. Its ratio to the comparison exponential remains exponential.

```formula
4^n = 2^{2n} = 2^n × 2^n
4^n / 2^n = 2^n → ∞
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
→: "tends to" as n grows
∞: infinity: growing without limit
In words: Correct: this does not have the bound. Its ratio to the comparison exponential remains exponential.
```

workedExample:
Divide each candidate by the base-two exponential and see whether the result stays bounded:

```formula
2^{n+1} / 2^n = 2
(2^n + n^5) / 2^n = 1 + n^5 / 2^n → 1
n^10 / 2^n → 0
4^n / 2^n = 2^n → ∞
100^{10} / 2^{100} ≈ 7.9 × 10^{-11}
100^{10} = 10^{20}
2^{100} ≈ 1.3 × 10^{30}
where
n: the input size, a positive whole number
2^n, 4^n: 2 or 4 raised to the power n
2^{n+1}: n + 1 copies of 2 multiplied together, which is 2 × 2^n
n^5, n^10: 5 or 10 copies of n multiplied together
→: "tends to" as n grows
∞: infinity: growing without limit
≈: approximately equal
In words: the first three ratios settle to a fixed number, so those functions are O(2^n); the last ratio grows forever, so 4^n is not.
```

For the tenth-power candidate at 100 items, the numerical substitution in the card shows a tiny ratio.

Adding one to the exponent multiplies by a constant; doubling the exponent squares the function.
